content: The respiratory examination is a critical component of a physical examination, particularly when a patient presents with respiratory symptoms such as dyspnea (shortness of breath), cough, or chest pain, or when their medical history suggests a potential lung pathology. Position, Lighting, and Draping: Position: The patient should be seated upright during the examination, with their hands resting at their sides. When examining the back, the patient is typically asked to move their arms forward into a self-hugging position to allow better access to the upper lung fields by moving the scapulae out of the way. Lighting: The lighting should be adjusted to ensure optimal visibility for the examiner. Draping: The chest should be fully exposed for the examination, but the exposure time should be minimized to ensure patient comfort and privacy. Steps of the Respiratory Examination: The respiratory examination follows the mnemonic IPPA: 1. Inspection 2. Palpation 3. Percussion 4. Auscultation General Physical Examination: Assess whether the patient is well-oriented to time, place, and person. Use the mnemonic PICKLE to evaluate for: Pallor (pale skin) Icterus (yellowing of the skin or eyes) Cyanosis (bluish discoloration of the skin, indicating hypoxia) Clubbing (enlargement of the fingertips, often associated with chronic hypoxia) Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails, often linked to iron deficiency anemia) Lymphadenopathy (enlarged lymph nodes) Edema (swelling due to fluid accumulation) Inspection: Evaluate the patient’s body mass for signs of wasting, cachexia, or puffiness. Look for the presence of medical instruments such as inhalers, peak flow meters, or oxygen cylinders. Examine the hands for: Flapping tremor (asterixis), which may indicate CO2 narcosis. Nicotine staining. Palpate the pulse while simultaneously observing the respiratory rate to prevent the patient from becoming conscious of their breathing pattern. Check for pulsus paradoxus, which may be seen in conditions like COPD. Assess the rhythm of the pulse, as atrial fibrillation (AF) can be associated with pneumonia. Inspect the nasal cavity for flaring of the alae nasi, which suggests labored breathing. Examine the oral cavity for nicotine staining on the inner surfaces or teeth. Evaluate the neck for: Tracheal deviation, which may indicate tension pneumothorax. Dilated neck vessels or abnormal pulsations. Absence of supraclavicular or infraclavicular fullness or visible swelling. Chest Examination: Stand at the foot of the patient to observe the chest. Identify the apex of the chest. Look for abnormal chest movements or pulsations. Assess the use of accessory muscles of respiration, such as the scalene and sternocleidomastoid muscles. Check for any chest deformities, swelling, or scars. Evaluate for spinal deformities: Kyphosis: An anterior-posterior curvature of the spine causing a forward-bent posture. Scoliosis: A lateral curvature of the spine, which may cause asymmetry in shoulder height. Barrel chest: An increased anterior-posterior diameter of the chest wall, often seen in COPD due to hyperinflation. Pectus excavatum: A congenital posterior displacement of the lower sternum, giving the chest a hollowed-out appearance. Pectus carinatum: A protrusion of the sternum. Signs of Respiratory Distress: Cyanosis: A bluish discoloration of the skin, indicating hypoxia. Pursed-lip breathing: Common in COPD, used to increase end-expiratory pressure. Use of accessory muscles: Indicates increased respiratory effort. Diaphragmatic paradox: The diaphragm moves in the opposite direction during inspiration, which may suggest a flail chest segment in trauma. Intercostal indrawing: Retraction of the intercostal spaces during inspiration, indicating labored breathing. Palpation: Check for localized temperature rise, tenderness, or subcutaneous emphysema. Assess for supraclavicular fullness. Evaluate tracheal position to ensure it is midline. Perform tactile fremitus by asking the patient to say boy-oh-boy or ninety-nine while using the ulnar aspect of the hand to detect changes in sound conduction. Assess respiratory expansion to ensure it is symmetrical. Locate the apex beat to check for any deviation of the heart. Percussion: Use the middle finger of one hand to strike the middle phalanx of the other hand’s middle finger. Compare the sides of the chest for differences in resonance: Dullness suggests consolidation. Hyper-resonance suggests pneumothorax. Measure diaphragmatic excursion, which is normally 3 to 6 cm. Auscultation: Listen for: Inspiratory crackles: May indicate decompensated congestive heart failure. Expiratory wheezes: Common in asthma or emphysema. Stridor: Indicates upper airway obstruction. Differences between bronchial and vesicular breath sounds. The ratio of inspiration to expiration time, which is prolonged in COPD. Vocal fremitus tests (e.g., egophony, whisper pectoriloquy) may be performed if needed. Other Systems Evaluation: Ideally, a cardiovascular and abdominal examination should also be conducted to provide a comprehensive assessment. Respiratory System Anatomy: The main lobes of the lungs are identified as: RUL: Right Upper Lobe LUL: Left Upper Lobe RML: Right Middle Lobe RLL: Right Lower Lobe LLL: Left Lower Lobe Specific Findings: Pectus excavatum: A congenital posterior displacement of the lower sternum, giving the chest a hollowed appearance. A lateral chest X-ray may show a subtle concave appearance of the lower sternum. Barrel chest: Associated with emphysema and lung hyperinflation. A lateral chest X-ray demonstrates increased anterior-posterior diameter and diaphragmatic flattening. Kyphosis: Causes forward bending of the spine. X-rays show extreme curvature. Scoliosis: A lateral curvature of the spine, often causing asymmetry in shoulder height. X-rays reveal pronounced curvature.
